Quick Answer

Overtime is 1.5× your regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek — at $30 an hour, overtime pays $45 an hour.

Overtime pay is one of the most powerful financial levers available to hourly workers, nurses, tradespeople, and shift employees. It turns an ordinary paycheck into an aggressive tool for eliminating debt, building emergency savings, or funding major family goals. Yet overtime is also one of the most frequently misunderstood and miscalculated line items on modern American pay stubs.

Every week at Hourly Wage Converter, we hear from workers who clocked 48 or 52 hours expecting a massive paycheck, only to feel blindsided on payday when their net direct deposit looks lighter than expected. Sometimes the confusion stems from payroll software withholding higher estimated taxes on a single large paycheck; other times, employers fail to properly calculate the FLSA "regular rate of pay" when shift differentials or production bonuses are involved.

Whether you are checking your employer's payroll accuracy, evaluating a new job offer with scheduled overtime, or planning your monthly budget, calculating overtime should never be guesswork. In this guide, we walk through the exact mechanics of time-and-a-half, examine California daily double-time rules, break down the complex "blended rate" formula for bonuses, and show you how to audit your overtime earnings with complete confidence.

The 40-Hour Workweek Rule: How Federal FLSA Overtime Actually Works

In the United States, overtime compensation is anchored in the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), codified under 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1). The fundamental statutory mandate is simple:

The Federal Overtime Mandate:

Covered non-exempt employees who work more than 40 physical hours in a defined 7-day workweek must receive compensation for all hours worked beyond 40 at a rate of not less than one and one-half times (1.5×) their regular rate of pay.

Applying this law correctly requires keeping three legal realities in mind:

  • The Defined 7-Day Workweek: Under 29 CFR § 778.105, a workweek is a fixed, regularly recurring period of 168 consecutive hours (seven 24-hour periods). It does not have to match Sunday-to-Saturday. Your employer can set it from Wednesday morning to the following Tuesday night. Once established, it remains permanent.
  • Physical Hours Worked Only: Only actual physical hours on the clock count toward the 40-hour threshold. Paid time off (PTO), sick leave, and paid holidays do not count toward statutory overtime under federal law unless required by a union contract.
  • Overtime Cannot Be Waived: Employees cannot legally sign away overtime rights. Even if you voluntarily agree to work extra hours at straight-time pay, that agreement is legally void, and your employer remains liable for back wages.

The Biweekly Averaging Trap: Why 80 Hours Across Two Weeks Fails

One of the most frequent payroll violations we encounter involves biweekly averaging. Because millions of employees are paid every two weeks, employers sometimes assume overtime only kicks in after working 80 hours across the pay period. That practice is strictly illegal under federal law (29 CFR § 778.104).

Under the FLSA, each 7-day workweek stands completely alone. Overtime cannot be averaged across two or more workweeks.

Worked Example: The Biweekly Averaging Trap

Consider an hourly employee earning $22.00 per hour on a biweekly payroll cycle:

  • Week 1: Employee works 45 hours during a heavy shift schedule.
  • Week 2: Employee works 35 hours during a slow period.
  • Total Hours in Pay Period: 45 + 35 = 80 hours.

The Illegal Employer Method (80-Hour Averaging):

Employer calculates 80 total hours × $22.00 = $1,760.00 gross pay with zero overtime.

The Legally Required FLSA Calculation:

  • Week 1 Pay: (40 regular hrs × $22.00) + (5 OT hrs × $33.00) = $880.00 + $165.00 = $1,045.00
  • Week 2 Pay: 35 regular hrs × $22.00 = $770.00
  • Correct Gross Paycheck: $1,045.00 + $770.00 = $1,815.00

Difference: The employee is legally owed an additional $55.00 on that paycheck. Over a year of fluctuating shifts, illegal averaging can easily deprive an hourly worker of over $1,400!

The Fundamental Overtime Formula: Time-and-a-Half (1.5×)

Calculating statutory overtime starts with the foundational time-and-a-half formula:

Overtime Hourly Rate = Base Hourly Wage × 1.5
Overtime Pay = Overtime Rate × Overtime Hours Worked (> 40 Hrs)
Total Gross Pay = (40 Regular Hours × Base Rate) + Overtime Pay

Alternatively, payroll systems often calculate pay by multiplying total hours worked by your base rate, then adding a 0.5× overtime premium for hours worked over 40:

Alternative Formula: Total Gross Pay = (Total Hours × Base Rate) + (Overtime Hours × Base Rate × 0.5)

Both mathematical paths produce the exact same penny-perfect gross total.

Scenario 1: Standard Hourly Worker ($24/Hour Working 48 Hours)

Let's examine a scenario representative of millions of logistics workers, tradespeople, and technicians: an employee earning $24.00 per hour who works 48 hours in a single 7-day workweek.

Step-by-Step Mathematical Breakdown:

  • Separate Regular and Overtime Hours: Out of 48 total hours, 40 hours represent standard straight-time, and 8 hours (48 − 40) qualify for statutory time-and-a-half.
  • Calculate Regular Straight-Time Earnings: 40 hours × $24.00 = $960.00.
  • Determine Overtime Hourly Rate (1.5×): $24.00 × 1.5 = $36.00 per hour.
  • Calculate Overtime Earnings: 8 hours × $36.00 = $288.00.
  • Calculate Total Gross Weekly Pay: $960.00 + $288.00 = $1,248.00.

To see how consistent overtime scales over longer time horizons:

  • Biweekly Paycheck Gross: $1,248.00 × 2 = $2,496.00 (compared to $1,920.00 without overtime).
  • Monthly Average Gross: ($1,248.00 × 52) ÷ 12 = $5,408.00 per month.
  • Annualized Gross Income: $1,248.00 × 52 weeks = $64,896.00 per year.

Working 8 overtime hours per week increases annual gross earnings from $49,920.00 to $64,896.00—delivering an extra $14,976.00 in gross pre-tax income. You can compare this earning power with our detailed wage benchmarks for $23 an hour and $30 an hour.

Scenario 2: Double Time (2.0×) & California Daily Overtime Laws

Federal FLSA regulations mandate 1.5× time-and-a-half, but federal law does not require double-time (2.0×) pay. However, several states and union collective bargaining agreements enforce strict daily overtime thresholds. The most notable example is California under California Labor Code § 510.

1.5× Daily OT

Over 8 Hours in a Workday

In California, Alaska, and Nevada, non-exempt employees earn 1.5× for all hours worked beyond 8 up to 12 in a single workday.

2.0× Double Time

Over 12 Hours in a Workday

In California, all hours worked beyond 12 in a single workday must be compensated at twice (2.0×) the employee's regular rate.

7th Day Rule

Consecutive Workdays

On the 7th consecutive day of work in a single workweek, California mandates 1.5× for the first 8 hours and 2.0× for hours past 8.

Consider a California worker earning $24.00 per hour who works a single 14-hour shift:

  • First 8 hours (Regular Straight-Time): 8 hrs × $24.00 = $192.00
  • Next 4 hours (1.5× Overtime Rate = $36.00/hr): 4 hrs × $36.00 = $144.00
  • Final 2 hours (2.0× Double-Time Rate = $48.00/hr): 2 hrs × $48.00 = $96.00
  • Total Shift Gross Pay: $192.00 + $144.00 + $96.00 = $432.00

Under federal FLSA rules in states without daily thresholds (such as Texas or Florida), that single 14-hour shift would only pay straight time ($336.00) unless total hours across the entire week exceeded 40. Knowing your state labor laws ensures you receive every dollar you are entitled to.

Scenario 3: The "Blended Rate" Rule for Bonuses & Shift Differentials

One of the most complex areas of payroll law involves the Regular Rate of Pay under FLSA Section 7(e). Many workers and payroll clerks mistakenly believe overtime is always calculated strictly on your base hourly rate.

Under federal law (29 CFR § 778.208), if an employee receives nondiscretionary bonuses (attendance incentives, production bonuses, safety bonuses) or shift differentials (extra pay for graveyard or weekend shifts), those earnings must be included in the regular rate before calculating the overtime premium.

Worked Example: Base Wage Plus Production Bonus

Suppose an employee earns a base rate of $20.00 per hour and works 45 hours during the week. In addition, the employee earns a $90.00 weekly production bonus.

The Common (and Illegal) Payroll Error:

Payroll multiplies only the base wage by 1.5: (40 hrs × $20.00) + (5 OT hrs × $30.00) + $90.00 bonus = $800.00 + $150.00 + $90.00 = $1,040.00.

The Correct FLSA Blended Rate Calculation:

  1. Calculate Total Straight-Time Compensation: (45 total hours × $20.00 base) + $90.00 bonus = $900.00 + $90.00 = $990.00.
  2. Calculate True Regular Rate of Pay: $990.00 total straight-time ÷ 45 total hours = $22.00 per hour (not $20.00!).
  3. Calculate Additional Overtime Premium (0.5×): Because straight time has already been paid for all 45 hours, the employee is owed an additional half-time premium on the 5 overtime hours: 5 hrs × ($22.00 × 0.5) = 5 hrs × $11.00 = $55.00.
  4. Calculate Total Weekly Gross Pay: $990.00 straight-time + $55.00 overtime premium = $1,045.00.

Difference: The employee legally earns $1,045.00 rather than $1,040.00. That extra $5.00 per week adds up to $260.00 per year in legally protected earnings.

Debunking the Myth: Why Overtime Check Taxes Spike (And Why You Never Lose Money)

One of the most persistent financial misconceptions heard in breakrooms is that "working overtime puts you into a higher tax bracket and makes you lose money."

Let's debunk this definitively: Working overtime will never cause you to take home less total money.

The confusion arises from how payroll tax withholding software operates compared to your actual year-end tax liability:

How Withholding Software Operates

Automated payroll systems calculate federal withholding by annualizing each paycheck individually (multiplying a biweekly check by 26). When a heavy overtime check looks like an $80,000 annualized salary instead of your typical $50,000, software temporarily withholds taxes at the 22% bracket on that check.

How Progressive Tax Brackets Work

The U.S. tax code uses progressive marginal brackets. For 2026, the standard deduction protects your first $16,100 (single) or $32,200 (married filing jointly) at a 0% tax rate. When your annual earnings enter a higher tax tier, only the dollars inside that upper tier are taxed at the higher rate. All dollars below that threshold remain taxed at 0%, 10%, or 12%. You keep the majority of every single overtime dollar worked.

When you file your annual tax return, the IRS reconciles your true total annual earnings. Any excess withholding from peak overtime pay periods is refunded directly to your pocket! For a complete step-by-step breakdown of paycheck withholdings, FICA payroll taxes, and 2026 tax brackets, read our comprehensive guide on how to calculate taxes on a paycheck.

For tax years 2025–2028 there is also a new federal deduction aimed specifically at overtime: many workers can deduct the premium half of their time-and-a-half pay when they file. See our guide to the no tax on overtime deduction for who qualifies, the caps, and how the premium pay is reported. A companion deduction in the same law covers tipped income — up to $25,000 a year; see our no tax on tips guide for its occupation list and phase-outs.

Common Employer & Employee Overtime Mistakes to Watch For

Over years of building wage and payroll tools at Hourly Wage Converter, we have analyzed countless pay stub discrepancies. In most situations, missing wages stem from six common errors:

1. Biweekly 80-Hour Averaging

Averaging 46 hours in Week 1 and 34 hours in Week 2 to show 80 total hours with zero overtime. Each 7-day workweek stands strictly alone under federal law.

2. Counting PTO Toward 40 Hours

Expecting overtime pay when you had 8 hours of holiday pay and 36 physical hours worked. FLSA overtime applies strictly to physical hours on the clock.

3. Misclassifying Non-Exempt Workers

Placing workers on modest salaries with managerial titles while assigning routine operational duties to improperly deny overtime compensation.

4. Excluding Bonuses from Regular Rate

Failing to include attendance bonuses, production bonuses, and shift differentials in the FLSA blended regular rate calculation.

5. Off-the-Clock Pre/Post Shift Work

Requiring workers to arrive 15 minutes early for shift prep or stay late to sanitize workstations without logging compensable clock time.

6. Illegal Comp Time in Private Sector

Offering informal "future time off" instead of cash overtime wages. In the private sector, comp time is strictly prohibited under federal law.

Frequently Asked Questions About Overtime Pay

How does an overtime calculator work?

An overtime calculator multiplies your standard hours (typically up to 40 hours per 7-day workweek) by your base hourly wage to determine regular earnings. It then isolates all hours worked beyond 40 and multiplies those extra hours by your statutory overtime rate—typically 1.5× for time-and-a-half or 2.0× for double time. Finally, it combines both sums to produce your total gross paycheck and projects your annual overtime earnings.

How do you calculate time-and-a-half manually?

To calculate time-and-a-half manually, multiply your base hourly wage by 1.5 to establish your overtime hourly rate. Next, multiply that rate by the number of overtime hours worked in the workweek. For example, at $24.00 per hour, your overtime rate is $36.00 ($24 × 1.5). If you work 8 overtime hours, your overtime earnings equal $288.00 (8 × $36.00). Added to your regular 40-hour base pay of $960.00, your total weekly gross pay is $1,248.00.

Can an employer average hours over two weeks in a biweekly pay period to avoid overtime?

No. Under federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) regulations (29 CFR § 778.104), each 7-day workweek stands strictly alone. An employer cannot average hours across two weeks. For example, if you work 45 hours in Week 1 and 35 hours in Week 2 of a biweekly pay period, you are legally entitled to 5 hours of overtime pay for Week 1, even though your two-week total equals 80 hours.

Does paid time off (PTO) or holiday pay count toward the 40-hour overtime threshold?

No. Under federal law, statutory overtime is triggered strictly by physical hours actually worked on the job. If you take 8 hours of paid holiday or vacation on Monday and work 36 physical hours Tuesday through Friday, your total paid hours equal 44, but you receive 44 straight-time hours with zero overtime pay because physical hours worked did not exceed 40.

Does working overtime push you into a higher tax bracket and make you lose money?

No, this is a pervasive payroll myth. The United States uses a progressive marginal tax bracket system. When extra overtime pay crosses into a higher tax bracket, only the specific dollars earned above that threshold are taxed at the higher marginal rate. All income below the bracket threshold remains taxed at lower rates. Working overtime will always increase your total take-home pay.

When does double time apply instead of time-and-a-half?

Federal law only requires time-and-a-half for hours over 40 in a workweek, so double time is not a federal rule — it comes from state law, union contracts, or employer policy. The best-known example is California, where non-exempt employees earn double time for hours over 12 in a single workday, and for hours over 8 on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek. Check your state rules and your employer policy before assuming a rate, and use the overtime calculator with a 2.0 multiplier to model double-time hours.

Key Takeaways & Your Overtime Paycheck Action Plan

Working overtime requires dedicating personal hours, energy, and physical stamina to your job. In return, the law guarantees you clear, enhanced compensation. Safeguarding your earnings comes down to disciplined habits:

Your 4-Step Paycheck Audit Checklist:

  • 1. Identify Your Employer's Workweek: Verify the exact day and hour your company's official 7-day payroll workweek begins and ends.
  • 2. Track Compensable Clock Time: Keep an independent log of your daily punch-in, lunch, and punch-out times on your smartphone or personal notebook.
  • 3. Verify the Blended Regular Rate: If you receive night differentials, hazard pay, or nondiscretionary bonuses, ensure your overtime multiplier is applied to your blended regular rate rather than your base rate.
  • 4. Pre-Calculate Before Payday: Run your numbers through our free Overtime Calculator or Homepage Converter and cross-reference your gross pay against your actual pay stub.

To project what your overtime pay looks like after federal withholding, FICA, and state taxes, test our companion guides on how to calculate taxes on a paycheck, explore our Hourly to Salary Calculator, or convert your annual earnings back to hourly with our Salary to Hourly Calculator.

Overtime rules may vary under state labor codes, prevailing wage statutes, and union collective bargaining agreements. Consult a qualified payroll specialist, labor attorney, or the U.S. Department of Labor for guidance on specific workplace disputes.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The FLSA threshold is 40 hours in a workweek; only hours beyond it earn the overtime premium.
  2. Under California’s daily rule, double time (2×) applies — $60 an hour on a $30 base rate.
  3. Blended rates apply when you work at different rates in the same week — the overtime rate is based on the weighted average, not just your base rate.
